title: Audit logs & admin activity review with Prism Analytics
summary: Customer asked for detailed coverage of Redwood audit logging: what's captured, export/ingest options, retention levels, KMS integration, and evidence for SOC2/ISO. We validated default retention and showed enterprise export paths (S3, syslog, streaming), discussed encryption at rest/in transit and KMS/HSM support, and agreed next steps to share SOC2 report and a short benchmark for SIEM ingestion. Action: Jordan to send security pack and sample log schema; Samir to provision short proof-of-concept for S3 export and syslog ingestion.
topics: RBAC / SSO / SAML events in logs

transcript:
Meeting header
Date/Time: 2026-03-28 15:00 UTC
Duration: 52 minutes
Attendees: Jordan Mills (Redwood AE), Samir Patel (Redwood SE), Lisa Cheng (Prism - Head of Security), Marco Ruiz (Prism - Platform Eng), Anita Desai (CISO)

Summary (auto): go over audit logs and admin activity, export options, retention and KMS.

[00:00] Jordan: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. Jordan from Redwood, I'm the AE on this. Samir, do you want to intro?
[00:08] Samir: Yeah hi, Samir Patel, SE. We'll go through what we capture in audit logs and the export/ingest options. We'll leave time for questions and then next steps.
[00:20] Lisa: Great, thanks. We're primarily focused on proving we can satisfy SOC2 and our regulatory retention needs. A few specific asks: what's in the logs for admin actions, can we export to our S3 bucket or stream to Splunk, and how long can you keep logs? Also how does KMS tie in.
[00:38] Jordan: Perfect, that's exactly what we planned. Quick note - sorry if audio is messy, I have a slight echo, we're good though.
[00:45] Samir: Okay jumping in. High level, Redwood audit logs capture three broad classes: administrative control plane events, API/request events, and system-level platform events.
[01:02] Samir: Examples: admin logins, role and RBAC changes, SSO/SAML configuration changes, API key creation and revocation, model version rollouts, keystore/KMS bindings, exports triggered, retention policy changes, and data export events. We also log request metadata: request id, user id, model id, token counts, region, latency and error codes.
[01:25] Marco: Do you log the prompt contents or outputs? That's our main privacy concern.
[01:32] Samir: Good question. By default prompt and output content is not stored in audit logs. The audit logs record metadata about requests. For content retention we have separate request logs and you can opt-in or be subject to your configured retention and redaction. Also there's field-level redaction so you can remove PII before it lands in long-term storage.
[01:54] Anita: So we get an audit trail of admin activity but not the raw prompt unless we enable request logging, correct?
[02:01] Jordan: Correct. Audit logs are designed for admin/operational actions and request metadata only. If you need full request bodies for debugging, that's a separate export with explicit customer consent and controls.
[02:12] Lisa: For SOC 2 evidence we need immutable admin activity and tamper-evident export. Do you integrate with KMS/HSM for signing or at least for encrypting exports?
[02:23] Samir: We support customer-managed KMS keys (AWS KMS, GCP Cloud KMS, Azure Key Vault) for encryption at rest of exported logs. For tamper evidence, exports to S3 can include MD5/SHA digests and we support object-lock / WORM via customer bucket settings to satisfy immutability requirements. For HSM-backed signing that's on our roadmap; currently customers can route logs to a customer-controlled ingestion pipeline (e.g., an intermediate service that signs) if they require HSM-based signatures.
[02:55] Marco: How do we actually get logs? Push or pull?
[02:58] Samir: We have multiple options: 1) Periodic batch export to customer S3 (signed, encrypted), 2) Real-time streaming via HTTP/S webhook or Kafka connectors, 3) Syslog / TCP/UDP forward to your SIEM (we support RFC5424-ish formats), and 4) API endpoints to pull logs.
[03:17] Lisa: For Splunk we prefer consuming via HTTP Event Collector or S3 ingestion. Does Redwood have tested Splunk HEC examples?
[03:24] Samir: Yes we've tested HEC. We'll share a sample HEC config. We also have docs for Splunk DBX and recommended field mappings.
[03:31] Jordan: Also worth noting we include structured fields for common SIEMs: event_type, actor, actor_ip, action, resource_type, resource_id, request_id, timestamp, outcome (success/fail), and extra metadata.
[03:46] [crosstalk briefly]
[03:50] Lisa: Retention — default is how long?
[03:53] Samir: Default platform retention for audit logs is 90 days for hosted standard customers. For enterprise customers you can extend to 7 years (or custom retention windows) if you have a dedicated contract. We also support legal hold mode which suspends deletion for a given window.
[04:10] Anita: Are deletions logged as events? We need proof that something was changed or deleted.
[04:15] Samir: Yes, deletion actions generate audit events (actor, timestamp, reason, request id). If legal hold is enabled we mark objects as immutably retained and deletion attempts will fail and generate an alert event.
[04:27] Marco: What about RBAC granularity in logs - do you capture role assignment changes down to the resource level?
[04:33] Samir: We capture role assignment events and include before/after states where applicable. There are examples in the schema we will share. Sometimes the transcription of long JSON diffs is heavy, so we capture a diff summary and provide links to full change artifacts stored in a secure object location.
[04:50] Lisa: For SSO/SAML events - do you log IdP assertions or just the event that a user authenticated?
[04:56] Samir: We log SAML/Sso events as authentication events with metadata (assertion id, IdP, subject id, authentication method) but we do not store full assertions in audit logs. Assertions may be available transiently in request logs for troubleshooting but are purged per retention settings.
[05:11] Jordan: Marco, your team mentioned you want a short POC to validate ingestion into your SIEM and retention policy?
[05:18] Marco: Yes the two things: verify S3 export schema matches our parsers and that syslog stream can handle our throughput during peak. Also we want to test legal hold behavior.
[05:27] Samir: Sounds good. For throughput, our syslog-forwarder is buffered and supports burst buffering; we'll provide recommended TCP+TLS connection parameters. For S3, we can do multi-part uploads and prefixing to avoid hot partitions.
[05:40] Lisa: Encryption in transit?
[05:42] Samir: All streams and APIs use TLS 1.2+ with recommended ciphers. For syslog we recommend TLS over TCP; UDP is supported but not recommended for critical logs.
[05:52] Anita: On KMS: who holds the keys? Customer-managed or Redwood-managed?
[05:56] Samir: You can choose customer-managed KMS. For hosted we also offer Redwood-managed keys if customers don't want to manage keys. When you choose customer-managed, Redwood never has plaintext access to the key material; we encrypt at the application level before storage.
[06:11] [00:06:11 timestamp - pause, background noise]
[06:20] Jordan: A couple of gotchas: 1) request logging (which includes prompt outputs) counts as data that may incur additional retention and encryption controls, 2) if you enable long-term request logging you need to verify PII handling and GDPR/data resident constraints, 3) if you want model-level change history that's captured only for rollout events, not every token.
[06:45] Lisa: Data residency — can we keep logs in eu-west-1 only?
[06:49] Samir: Yes, regional export endpoints are available. We can route exports to a regional S3 and ensure logs are stored only in the specified region. For multi-region redundancy we can replicate based on policy but that would be a separate configuration.
[07:03] Marco: On schema - can you share a sample event payload?
[07:06] Samir: We'll attach the schema to the security pack. Quick example: {event_type: "admin_change", actor: "user:anita@prism.com", action: "role_update", resource: "project:pii-processing", before: "role:user", after: "role:admin", timestamp: "..."} — note schema in doc will be JSON-LD-ish.
[07:25] Lisa: That example contains identifiers - is there an option to hash or pseudonymize actor ids?
[07:30] Samir: Yes you can enable hashing/pseudonymization on export. We support field-level transforms during export (SHA256, redaction, tokenization). We'll show config snippets.
[07:40] Jordan: Question from my side — do you need a list of Redwood roles to map to your internal roles?
[07:45] Marco: Yes please, we want role mapping and a crosswalk doc.
[07:48] Jordan: We'll include that.
[07:50] [08:00] Lisa: For SOC2 we need attestable logs. Where can we pull evidence?
[08:05] Samir: You can export logs on-demand for audit windows. We provide an audit export tool that zips and signs exports and includes an evidence manifest. We'll share the process. We also provide our SOC2 report and operator logs in the security pack.
[08:20] Anita: How do you handle operator access on Redwood side? We need to see operator actions in our tenant.
[08:26] Samir: Operator actions are logged with an operator tag and are visible to the tenant's security admins. We separate operator namespace and mark events as operator-initiated. Access is governed by Redwood internal RBAC and documented in the SOC 2 controls.
[08:39] Lisa: Are there pre-built connectors for major SIEMs?
[08:42] Samir: Yes — Splunk, Datadog, Sumo Logic, Elastic, and common syslog/S3 patterns. We'll share tested config.
[08:51] Marco: Performance during peak - can you insert sample throughput numbers?
[08:55] Samir: For a medium enterprise setup we commonly see sustained 2k events/sec to syslog endpoints and bursts to 10k+/sec with appropriate buffering. We'll run a short benchmark for your cluster.
[09:07] [09:10] Lisa: On cost — do exports incur egress costs?
[09:13] Jordan: Exports to customer-owned S3 in the same cloud/region won't have egress. Cross-region replication and streaming to external systems may have standard egress charges per cloud provider; we'll include cost guidance.
[09:25] Anita: For legal hold and retention overrides — who's responsible for initiating legal hold? Customer or Redwood?
[09:31] Samir: Either. Customers can set retention/hold via console or API. For enterprise we can set contractual holds if needed. All hold actions are auditable.
[09:40] Marco: Does the console allow fine-grained retention per project/environment?
[09:44] Samir: Yes you can set retention by project, environment, or tag. The defaults are org-level but overrides are supported.
[09:52] Lisa: Any pitfalls we should be aware of?
[09:55] Samir: A few: enabling request logging without redaction can surface sensitive data; exporting to third-party SIEMs requires careful mapping of event types; and expect some lead time on dedicated retention beyond default for enterprise agreements.
[10:10] Jordan: Quick demo note — we have a one-page checklist we'll share that lists necessary IAM roles, KMS policy examples, S3 bucket settings (object-lock, versioning), and recommended syslog TLS config.
[10:22] Lisa: Great. If we want automated alerts — does Redwood generate security alert events?
[10:27] Samir: We have built-in alerts (suspicious login patterns, repeated failed auth, unusual export patterns) and you can pipe those alerts to webhook or SIEM. Alerts are also logged as audit events.
[10:39] Anita: Are there retention certifications or attestations for encrypted backups?
[10:43] Samir: We'll include details in SOC2 and ISO artifact pack. For backups we describe encryption, key management, and rotation policies.
[10:51] [10:55] Marco: Can we do a quick review of the log field names so I can check our parsers?
[10:59] Samir: Sure. event_type, actor, actor_type, actor_ip, action, target_type, target_id, request_id, outcome, timestamp, source_region, user_agent, extras. We'll send the canonical schema as JSON and CSV examples.
[11:18] Lisa: Will the logs include redacted prompt hashes if we turn on request logging?
[11:22] Samir: Yes you can store prompt hashes (deterministic) instead of full text to allow deduping without exposing content.
[11:30] Jordan: Okay I want to summarize next steps — Jordan to send security pack and SOC2 report, Samir to stand up S3 export and syslog demo, Marco to provide retention/legal-hold requirements.
[11:42] Lisa: And please include the sample Splunk HEC config and the event schema.
[11:47] Jordan: Will do. Anything else?
[11:50] [brief pause]
[11:53] Anita: Can we get a timeline for the POC?
[11:55] Samir: We'll aim to have the POC available by 2026-04-03, then a follow-up the week of 2026-04-06 to review results.
[12:05] Jordan: Great. Thanks everyone.
[12:08] Lisa: Thanks.
[12:10] End of meeting.

Notes: transcript may contain minor mis-transcriptions (IdP spelled as IdP/Id p, KV cache referred to as K V cache etc.). References to artifacts: security pack link (sent after call), sample schema (attached), Splunk HEC snippets (attached).
